subject: chemistry
topicDisplay: Structure 1.1–1.3 — particles, the nuclear atom and electron configurations
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {subject} question that tests this idea: "{lo}". Then mark my answer the way an IB examiner would.
promptWeak: Explain this {board} {subject} idea simply, with a worked example and the most common mistake students make: "{lo}".

learningObjectives.title: Elements, compounds and mixtures, and how mixtures are separated
Particles in motion: states of matter and changes of state
Temperature measures average kinetic energy; converting Celsius and kelvin
Counting protons, neutrons and electrons from the nuclear symbol
Isotopes and relative atomic mass from abundances
How atoms emit light, and what colour, wavelength and energy mean
What the hydrogen spectrum proves about energy levels
How many electrons each main level can hold
Sublevels and the shapes of s and p orbitals
Writing electron configurations with Aufbau, Pauli and Hund
From the convergence limit to ionization energy, and the trends in it
Reading successive ionization energies for the group

questions.q: Impure solid X is dissolved in the minimum volume of hot water, and the hot solution is filtered. When the filtrate is cooled, crystals of X form. Why do crystals of X form when the solution is cooled?
options: X freezes, as the solution is cooled below the temperature at which X melts
X is less soluble in cold water than in hot water, so the excess comes out of solution
Dissolved X sinks and collects at the bottom of the flask as the water cools
Water evaporates as it cools, since the solubility of X does not change
optionWhy: A student who confuses dissolving with melting picks this. X was never molten: it was dissolved in the water, and the solution was never near the melting point of X. It crystallizes because its solubility falls.
The hot solution is close to saturated. Cold water can dissolve less X, so on cooling the X that the water can no longer hold crystallizes. The small amounts of soluble impurity stay dissolved.
A student who thinks dissolved solids settle picks this. A solution stays uniform; dissolved X does not sink. Crystals form only once the cold water cannot hold all the X in solution.
A student who thinks solubility does not depend on temperature picks this. Little water evaporates from a cooling solution. Crystals form because X is much less soluble in cold water than in hot.
questions.explain: The hot solution is close to saturated. Cold water can dissolve less X, so on cooling the X that the water can no longer hold crystallizes. The small amounts of soluble impurity stay dissolved.

questions.q: A student wants to recover all of the potassium chloride, as a solid, from a dilute aqueous solution of potassium chloride. Which method should be used?
options: Filtration, as the dissolved solid is held back on the paper
Cooling, as the dissolved solid freezes when cold enough
Evaporation, as the water escapes and the solid is left behind
Decanting, as the dissolved solid settles to the bottom on standing
optionWhy: A student who thinks filter paper can catch a dissolved solid picks this. Dissolved K⁺ and Cl⁻ ions pass through the paper with the water, so the filtrate is still potassium chloride solution.

A student who confuses dissolving with melting picks this. The potassium chloride is dissolved, not molten, so it cannot freeze. Cooling a dilute solution far enough freezes the water, not the dissolved salt.

Heating the solution in an open dish vaporizes the water, which escapes into the air; potassium chloride does not vaporize, so the solid is left in the dish. Evaporation recovers the solute; distillation would be used to collect the water.

A student who thinks a dissolved solid settles picks this. A solution is a homogeneous mixture; the dissolved ions stay evenly spread and never settle, so pouring off the liquid leaves no solid behind.
questions.explain: Heating the solution in an open dish vaporizes the water, which escapes into the air; potassium chloride does not vaporize, so the solid is left in the dish. Evaporation recovers the solute; distillation would be used to collect the water.

questions.q: A substance at room temperature has a fixed volume but takes the shape of its container. Which statement about its particles is correct?
options: They are close together but not in fixed positions
They are spaced about halfway between those of a solid and a gas
The spaces between the particles are filled with air
Each one is soft, so it changes shape as the substance flows
optionWhy: This is a liquid. Its particles are close together, as in a solid (liquids are barely compressible), but not held in fixed positions, so they move past one another and the liquid takes the shape of its container.

A student who pictures a liquid as halfway between a solid and a gas in spacing picks this. Liquid particles are almost as close as in a solid, which is why a liquid, like a solid, is hardly compressible.
A student who thinks there is air between particles picks this. The spaces between particles are empty. Air is itself made of particles, so it cannot fill the gaps between particles.
A student who gives particles the properties of the bulk substance picks this. A liquid flows because its particles move past one another; the particles themselves do not soften or change shape.
questions.explain: This is a liquid. Its particles are close together, as in a solid (liquids are barely compressible), but not held in fixed positions, so they move past one another and the liquid takes the shape of its container.

questions.q: Which change of state is correctly named and correctly represented by an equation with state symbols?
options: Melting: NaCl(s) → NaCl(aq)
Condensation: H₂O(g) → H₂O(s)
Boiling: H₂O(aq) → H₂O(g)
Sublimation: CO₂(s) → CO₂(g)
optionWhy: A student who thinks dissolving is melting picks this. NaCl(s) → NaCl(aq) represents dissolving in water. Melting would be NaCl(s) → NaCl(l), which needs a temperature of about 800 °C.

A student who calls any change from gas to a denser state condensation picks this. A direct change from gas to solid, as when frost forms, is deposition. Condensation is gas to liquid, H₂O(g) → H₂O(l).
A student who uses (aq) to mean any liquid picks this. (aq) means dissolved in water, so water itself is H₂O(l). Boiling is H₂O(l) → H₂O(g).

At atmospheric pressure solid carbon dioxide ('dry ice') changes directly into gas without becoming liquid. A direct change from solid to gas is sublimation, and the state symbols (s) and (g) show exactly that.
questions.explain: At atmospheric pressure solid carbon dioxide ('dry ice') changes directly into gas without becoming liquid. A direct change from solid to gas is sublimation, and the state symbols (s) and (g) show exactly that.

questions.q: A sample of neon gas is at 77 °C. It is heated until the average kinetic energy of its atoms has doubled. What is its new temperature? (T/K = T/°C + 273)
optionWhy: Average kinetic energy is proportional to temperature in kelvin. 77 °C = 350 K; doubling gives 700 K; 700 − 273 = 427 °C.

A student who takes average kinetic energy to be proportional to the Celsius temperature doubles 77 °C to get 154 °C. The Celsius zero is not absolute zero, so the temperature must be doubled in kelvin: 350 K → 700 K = 427 °C.
A student who calculates the new temperature in kelvin, 700 K, but does not convert it back gives 700 °C. The question asks for °C: 700 K = 700 − 273 = 427 °C.
A student who always adds 273 to convert gives 700 + 273 = 973 °C. Converting from kelvin to Celsius means subtracting 273: 700 K = 427 °C.
questions.explain: Average kinetic energy is proportional to temperature in kelvin. 77 °C = 350 K; doubling gives 700 K; 700 − 273 = 427 °C.
questions.working: Average Ek ∝ T (in K). T₁ = 77 + 273 = 350 K. Doubling the average kinetic energy doubles T: T₂ = 2 × 350 K = 700 K. In °C: 700 − 273 = 427 °C.

questions.q: How many neutrons are there in one atom of ⁸¹₃₅Br (mass number 81, atomic number 35)?
optionWhy: 35 is the number of protons (and of electrons in the neutral atom). The number of neutrons is not tied to the atomic number: it is A − Z = 81 − 35 = 46.
Correct. The mass number 81 counts the protons and neutrons; the atomic number 35 is the number of protons. Neutrons = A − Z = 81 − 35 = 46.
81 is the mass number, the total number of protons and neutrons. Subtract the 35 protons to get the neutrons: 81 − 35 = 46.

Subtracting 35 electrons as well as 35 protons treats the electrons as if they had a mass like a proton's and were counted in A. Electrons are not nucleons and their mass is negligible, so A counts only protons and neutrons: 81 − 35 = 46.
questions.explain: Correct. The mass number 81 counts the protons and neutrons; the atomic number 35 is the number of protons. Neutrons = A − Z = 81 − 35 = 46.
questions.working: Protons = Z = 35. Mass number A = protons + neutrons, so neutrons = A − Z = 81 − 35 = 46.

questions.q: Hydrogen (atomic number 1) has isotopes ¹H and ²H. Water made from ²H, D₂O, melts at 3.8 °C, boils at 101.4 °C and has a density of about 1.1 g cm⁻³; ordinary water, H₂O, melts at 0.0 °C, boils at 100.0 °C and has a density of about 1.0 g cm⁻³. Both react with sodium in the same way: H₂O forms NaOH and H₂, and D₂O forms NaOD and D₂. Which statement accounts for these observations?
options: D₂O molecules contain more electrons, so the forces between them are stronger.
Boiling D₂O breaks its O–D bonds, which need more energy to break than O–H bonds.
The extra neutrons in D₂O carry charge, so D₂O molecules attract one another more.
D₂O molecules are heavier than H₂O molecules, but have the same electron arrangement.
optionWhy: Both isotopes of hydrogen have atomic number 1, so a neutral atom of either has one electron, and H₂O and D₂O molecules both have 10 electrons. ²H differs from ¹H by one neutron; a change in the number of electrons would give an ion, not an isotope.

Boiling a molecular substance separates whole molecules by overcoming the intermolecular forces between them; no O–D or O–H covalent bonds break. So the strength of the bonds inside the molecules does not set the boiling point, and this statement also leaves the melting points and densities unexplained.
Neutrons have no charge, so the extra neutrons do not change the charge of the nucleus or the atom. They add mass only, and it is the difference in mass that changes the physical properties.

Correct. ¹H has 1 proton and no neutron; ²H has 1 proton and 1 neutron. The electron arrangement, which controls chemical reactions, is the same, so the reactions are the same. The greater mass changes mass-dependent physical properties: melting point, boiling point and density.
questions.explain: Correct. ¹H has 1 proton and no neutron; ²H has 1 proton and 1 neutron. The electron arrangement, which controls chemical reactions, is the same, so the reactions are the same. The greater mass changes mass-dependent physical properties: melting point, boiling point and density.

questions.q: Copper has two isotopes, copper-63 and copper-65, with relative isotopic masses 62.93 and 64.93. The relative atomic mass of copper is 63.55. What is the percentage abundance of copper-65?
optionWhy: (64.93 − 63.55) ÷ 2.00 = 0.690 is the fraction of copper-63, not copper-65. A_r lies closer to the more abundant isotope; 63.55 is closer to 62.93, so copper-65 must be the minor isotope.
Writing both abundances as x (62.93x + 64.93x = 6355) ignores the fact that the abundances add up to 100%. If copper-65 is x%, copper-63 is (100 − x)%.

Using the mass numbers 63 and 65 instead of the isotopic masses 62.93 and 64.93 gives (63.55 − 63) ÷ 2 = 0.275. The stem gives the relative isotopic masses; with them the fraction is 0.62 ÷ 2.00 = 0.310.
Correct. Let x% be copper-65: 64.93x + 62.93(100 − x) = 6355, so 2.00x = 62, x = 31.0. A check: A_r (63.55) is closer to 62.93, so copper-63 should be the more abundant isotope, as it is (69.0%).
questions.explain: Correct. Let x% be copper-65: 64.93x + 62.93(100 − x) = 6355, so 2.00x = 62, x = 31.0. A check: A_r (63.55) is closer to 62.93, so copper-63 should be the more abundant isotope, as it is (69.0%).

questions.q: The mass spectrum of element X, showing only the peaks from singly charged atomic ions (X⁺), has two peaks: m/z 79 (relative abundance 100) and m/z 81 (relative abundance 97.3). Atomic numbers: selenium 34, bromine 35, gadolinium 64, gold 79. Which element is X?
options: Element X is selenium (A_r 78.97).
Element X is gold (A_r 196.97).
Element X is bromine (A_r 79.90).
Element X is gadolinium (A_r 157.25).
optionWhy: This takes A_r as 79, the m/z of the tallest peak. The peak at m/z 81 is almost as tall, so the weighted mean is about 80, which matches bromine.
This reads m/z 79 as the atomic number. m/z of a singly charged ion is its relative mass, which is related to the mass number, not the atomic number. Gold atoms have masses near 197.
Correct. A_r = (79 × 100 + 81 × 97.3) ÷ (100 + 97.3) = 15 781.3 ÷ 197.3 = 79.99, which matches bromine (79.90) and no other option. The two peaks are two isotopes of nearly equal abundance.
Dividing 15 781.3 by 100 treats the relative abundances as percentages, but they add up to 197.3. The weighted mean of the two m/z values must lie between 79 and 81.
questions.explain: Correct. A_r = (79 × 100 + 81 × 97.3) ÷ (100 + 97.3) = 15 781.3 ÷ 197.3 = 79.99, which matches bromine (79.90) and no other option. The two peaks are two isotopes of nearly equal abundance.
questions.working: Σ(relative abundance) = 100 + 97.3 = 197.3. A_r = (79 × 100 + 81 × 97.3) ÷ 197.3 = (7900 + 7881.3) ÷ 197.3 = 79.99 → closest to bromine (A_r 79.90). (m/z values are whole numbers here, so the calculated value differs slightly from the accepted A_r.)

questions.q: Violet light and red light lie at opposite ends of the visible spectrum. How does violet light compare with red light?
options: Violet light has the lower frequency, as it has the shorter wavelength.
Violet light has the longer wavelength, as its photons carry more energy.
Violet photons carry less energy, as red is the colour of hot, energetic things.
Violet photons carry more energy, as violet light has the higher frequency.
optionWhy: Violet does have the shorter wavelength, but wavelength and frequency are inversely related, so the shorter wavelength of violet means a higher frequency, and therefore a greater photon energy, than red.
Violet photons do carry more energy, but more energetic photons have shorter wavelengths, not longer ones. Violet (about 400 nm) is shorter than red (about 700 nm).

Red is not the high-energy end of the visible spectrum; it is the low-energy end, next to infrared. Violet, next to ultraviolet, has the shorter wavelength, higher frequency and greater photon energy.
Violet light has a shorter wavelength than red, so it has a higher frequency, and photon energy increases with frequency. Violet photons therefore carry more energy than red photons.
questions.explain: Violet light has a shorter wavelength than red, so it has a higher frequency, and photon energy increases with frequency. Violet photons therefore carry more energy than red photons.

questions.q: White light from a hot filament lamp gives a continuous spectrum when it is passed through a prism. Light from a hydrogen discharge tube passed through the same prism gives a line spectrum. How does the line spectrum differ from the continuous spectrum?
options: It shows dark lines at certain wavelengths, across a continuous band of colour.
It shows only one bright line, since a hydrogen atom has only one electron.
It shows bright lines at only certain wavelengths, on a dark background.
It shows bright lines at frequencies spaced at equal intervals across it.
optionWhy: Dark lines across a continuous band make an absorption spectrum. The discharge tube emits light only at certain wavelengths, so its spectrum is bright lines on a dark background.

The lines are not produced one per electron. Each line comes from a different transition between energy levels, and the many atoms in the tube make many different transitions, so hydrogen gives several lines.

A continuous spectrum contains every wavelength over a range. The hydrogen atoms emit only photons of certain energies, so the line emission spectrum consists of separate bright lines at particular wavelengths with darkness between them.

The lines are not equally spaced in frequency, because the energy levels are not equally spaced. The levels get closer together at higher energy, so within each set the lines crowd together towards higher frequency.
questions.explain: A continuous spectrum contains every wavelength over a range. The hydrogen atoms emit only photons of certain energies, so the line emission spectrum consists of separate bright lines at particular wavelengths with darkness between them.

questions.q: In the hydrogen emission spectrum, transitions ending at n = 1 produce lines in the ultraviolet region. In which region are the lines produced by transitions ending at n = 3, and why?
options: Infrared, because the energy gaps from higher levels down to n = 3 are smaller than those down to n = 2
Ultraviolet, because n = 3 is a higher energy level than n = 2, so its photons carry more energy
Ultraviolet, because the levels above n = 3 are more widely spaced than the levels above n = 2
Visible, because the levels are equally spaced, so every fall releases the same size of energy step
optionWhy: The levels get closer together as n increases, so every fall ending at n = 3 releases less energy than any fall ending at n = 2, including the smallest (n = 3 → n = 2, the red line of the visible set). Lower photon energy means lower frequency and longer wavelength than visible light: the infrared region.

A photon’s energy is the difference between two levels, not the energy of the level the electron lands in. The gaps down to n = 3 are smaller than the gaps down to n = 2, so these lines are lower in energy than visible light: infrared.
The levels get closer together, not further apart, as n increases, even though the orbitals are further from the nucleus. The smaller gaps above n = 3 give lower-energy photons, in the infrared.

The levels are not equally spaced; their gaps shrink as n increases. Falls to n = 3 release less energy than falls to n = 2, so their lines lie beyond the red end of the visible spectrum, in the infrared.
questions.explain: The levels get closer together as n increases, so every fall ending at n = 3 releases less energy than any fall ending at n = 2, including the smallest (n = 3 → n = 2, the red line of the visible set). Lower photon energy means lower frequency and longer wavelength than visible light: the infrared region.

questions.q: The diagram shows part of the emission spectrum of hydrogen plotted against frequency. The four lines P, Q, R and S lie in the visible region, and the lines converge towards the limit marked L. Which electron transition produces line P?
optionWhy: An electron moving up from n = 2 to n = 3 absorbs energy; it does not emit a photon. Emission lines come from electrons falling to a lower level, so P, the lowest-frequency visible line, is the fall from n = 3 to n = 2.

A photon’s energy is the difference between the two levels, not the energy of the level the electron ends in. Falls to n = 1 are the largest and give ultraviolet lines, not the visible line P, which is the smallest fall into n = 2: from n = 3.

P has the lowest frequency, so it has the longest wavelength (red light, about 656 nm). A longer wavelength does not mean more energy: photon energy E = hf rises with frequency, so P carries the least energy of the four lines and comes from the smallest fall into n = 2, from n = 3. The fall from n = 6 to n = 2 is the largest of the four and gives S.

The visible lines of hydrogen are produced by electrons falling to n = 2. P is the line of lowest frequency, so it carries the least energy and comes from the smallest fall into n = 2, from n = 3. Larger falls (from n = 4, 5, 6 …) give the higher-frequency lines Q, R, S and the lines that crowd towards L.
questions.explain: The visible lines of hydrogen are produced by electrons falling to n = 2. P is the line of lowest frequency, so it carries the least energy and comes from the smallest fall into n = 2, from n = 3. Larger falls (from n = 4, 5, 6 …) give the higher-frequency lines Q, R, S and the lines that crowd towards L.
questions.working: Visible lines of hydrogen arise from transitions ending at n = 2. Photon energy E = hf, so the lowest-frequency line P is the smallest energy gap ending at n = 2, i.e. n = 3 → n = 2. Higher starting levels give higher-frequency lines that converge on L (n = ∞ → n = 2).

questions.q: A potassium atom (Z = 19) has the electron arrangement 2, 8, 8, 1: two electrons in the first main energy level, eight in the second, eight in the third and one in the fourth. Which statement about the third main energy level (n = 3) of this atom is correct?
options: It is not full, because a level with n = 3 can hold up to 2 × 3² = 18 electrons.
It is full, because every main energy level after the first holds a maximum of 8 electrons.
It is full, because electrons only enter the fourth level once the third holds all it can.
It is not full, because it has n² = 9 orbitals and so has room for one more electron.
optionWhy: The capacity of a main energy level is 2n², so the third level can hold 18 electrons (3s, 3p and 3d sublevels). Potassium’s third level holds only 8; its nineteenth electron enters the fourth level because 4s is lower in energy than 3d, not because n = 3 is full.

‘2, 8, 8’ describes the filling of the first 20 elements, not the capacity of the third level. Capacity is 2n²: the third level can hold 18 electrons, and in the elements after calcium it fills up to 18 (3s² 3p⁶ 3d¹⁰).

Levels are not always filled completely before the next begins. The 4s sublevel is lower in energy than 3d, so the nineteenth electron enters n = 4 while n = 3 still has ten empty places (its capacity is 2 × 3² = 18).
The third level does have n² = 9 orbitals, but each orbital holds two electrons of opposite spin, so the capacity is 2n² = 18, not 9. With 8 electrons present there is room for ten more, not one.
questions.explain: The capacity of a main energy level is 2n², so the third level can hold 18 electrons (3s, 3p and 3d sublevels). Potassium’s third level holds only 8; its nineteenth electron enters the fourth level because 4s is lower in energy than 3d, not because n = 3 is full.
questions.working: Maximum number of electrons in main energy level n = 2n². For n = 3: 2 × 3² = 18. The third level of potassium holds 8 of a possible 18, so it is not full; the nineteenth electron enters the fourth level (4s) because 4s is lower in energy than 3d, not because the third level is full.

questions.q: Which description of the shapes and orientations of the three 2p atomic orbitals is correct?
options: Three dumbbell shapes along the x, y and z axes, at 90° to one another
Three dumbbell shapes lying in one plane, at 120° to one another
Three figure-of-eight paths that the electrons follow around the nucleus
A single dumbbell shape that holds all six electrons of the 2p sublevel
optionWhy: Each p orbital is a dumbbell with two lobes on opposite sides of the nucleus. The three p orbitals of a sublevel point along the three perpendicular axes: px, py and pz.
The shape is right but the orientation is not. The p orbitals are not arranged by spreading apart like electron domains; they lie along the x, y and z axes, at 90° to one another.
Orbitals are not paths. Each p orbital is a dumbbell-shaped region where there is a high probability of finding an electron; the three lie along the x, y and z axes.
The 2p sublevel is not one orbital. It contains three separate p orbitals, each holding up to two electrons, directed along the x, y and z axes.
questions.explain: Each p orbital is a dumbbell with two lobes on opposite sides of the nucleus. The three p orbitals of a sublevel point along the three perpendicular axes: px, py and pz.

questions.q: In a potassium atom, the nineteenth electron occupies the 4s sublevel rather than the 3d sublevel. What is the reason?
options: The 4s orbital is nearer the nucleus, and orbitals fill from the inside outward.
Hund’s rule requires an s sublevel to be filled before any d sublevel.
The third main energy level is already full, as it holds at most eight electrons.
The 4s sublevel is lower in energy than the 3d sublevel in this atom.
optionWhy: Filling follows energy, not distance. The 4s orbital actually extends further from the nucleus than 3d; it fills first because, in potassium, it is lower in energy.

Hund’s rule is about orbitals of equal energy within one sublevel: they are singly occupied, with parallel spins, before pairing. The filling order of sublevels comes from the Aufbau principle and the sublevel energies.
The third level can hold 18 electrons, including ten in 3d; it is not full at eight. The 3d sublevel is simply higher in energy than 4s in potassium, and it fills later, from scandium onwards.
Electrons occupy the lowest-energy orbitals available (the Aufbau principle). In potassium and calcium, the 4s sublevel is lower in energy than 3d, so it fills first: potassium is [Ar] 4s¹.
questions.explain: Electrons occupy the lowest-energy orbitals available (the Aufbau principle). In potassium and calcium, the 4s sublevel is lower in energy than 3d, so it fills first: potassium is [Ar] 4s¹.

questions.q: An orbital (arrow-in-box) diagram is drawn for a ground-state nitrogen atom, 1s² 2s² 2p³. The 1s box and the 2s box each contain two arrows pointing in opposite directions. Which description of the 2p part of the diagram is correct?
options: Three boxes each hold one arrow, and all three arrows point the same way.
Three boxes: one holds two opposite arrows, one holds one, one is empty.
Three boxes each hold one arrow, and the middle arrow is reversed.
One box holds all three arrows, as the 2p sublevel is only one orbital.
optionWhy: By Hund’s rule, the three electrons occupy the three 2p orbitals singly, with parallel spins, before any orbital holds a pair. Each 2p box therefore contains one arrow, all pointing in the same direction.
Electrons do not pair while orbitals of equal energy are empty. Hund’s rule places one arrow in each of the three 2p boxes, all pointing the same way.
Opposite spins are required only for two electrons in the same orbital. Singly occupied orbitals of one sublevel have parallel spins, so all three arrows point the same way.
The 2p sublevel consists of three orbitals, drawn as three boxes, and no orbital can hold more than two electrons. The three electrons go one into each box, with parallel spins.
questions.explain: By Hund’s rule, the three electrons occupy the three 2p orbitals singly, with parallel spins, before any orbital holds a pair. Each 2p box therefore contains one arrow, all pointing in the same direction.

questions.q: The diagram shows four arrow-in-box diagrams, W, X, Y and Z, each drawn for the 3d sublevel of a ground-state iron atom, [Ar] 3d⁶ 4s². Which diagram is correct?
options: Diagram W
Diagram X
Diagram Y
Diagram Z
optionWhy: Filling three orbitals with pairs while two orbitals of the same energy stay empty breaks Hund’s rule. Electrons occupy each 3d orbital singly before any orbital holds a pair, so the ground state is ↑↓ ↑ ↑ ↑ ↑ (X).

By Hund’s rule the six 3d electrons first occupy the five orbitals singly with parallel spins; the sixth then pairs, with opposite spin, in one orbital (Pauli exclusion principle). X shows one paired box and four single up arrows.

Opposite spins are required only for two electrons in the same orbital. Singly occupied orbitals of one sublevel hold electrons with parallel spins, so the four single arrows all point the same way (X), not alternately up and down.

Two electrons in the same orbital must have opposite spins (Pauli exclusion principle); ↑↑ in one box is not allowed. Hund’s rule’s parallel spins apply to electrons in different orbitals, so the correct diagram is X: ↑↓ ↑ ↑ ↑ ↑.

questions.q: The first ionization energies (kJ mol⁻¹) of the period 2 elements are: Li 520, Be 900, B 801, C 1086, N 1402, O 1314, F 1681, Ne 2081. Which statement correctly explains both the fall from Be to B and the fall from N to O?
options: Be’s filled 2s sublevel and N’s half-filled 2p sublevel have a special stability that makes them harder to ionize.
B’s electron is in 2p, higher in energy than 2s; O’s is in a doubly occupied 2p orbital, where repulsion raises its energy.
B’s electron is in a doubly occupied 2p orbital, where repulsion raises its energy; O’s is in a higher sublevel than N’s.
B and O atoms are larger than Be and N atoms, so the electron removed is further from the nucleus in each case.
optionWhy: The explanations must be based on the energy of the electron removed, not on a 'special stability' of filled or half-filled sublevels. Boron’s electron is in the higher-energy 2p sublevel; oxygen’s is in a doubly occupied 2p orbital, raised in energy by repulsion.

Be is 1s² 2s² and B is 1s² 2s² 2p¹: boron’s electron is removed from the 2p sublevel, which is higher in energy than 2s. N is 2s² 2p³ with three singly occupied 2p orbitals; O is 2s² 2p⁴ with one 2p orbital holding a pair, and repulsion between the paired electrons raises the energy of the electron removed. In both cases less energy is needed.

The two explanations are the wrong way round. Boron has a single 2p electron, so pairing cannot apply; its electron is in 2p, above 2s. Nitrogen and oxygen both lose a 2p electron; oxygen’s comes from a doubly occupied orbital.

Atoms get smaller across a period: boron is smaller than beryllium and oxygen smaller than nitrogen. The falls are caused by the higher energy of the 2p sublevel (Be → B) and by electron-pair repulsion in a 2p orbital (N → O).
questions.explain: Be is 1s² 2s² and B is 1s² 2s² 2p¹: boron’s electron is removed from the 2p sublevel, which is higher in energy than 2s. N is 2s² 2p³ with three singly occupied 2p orbitals; O is 2s² 2p⁴ with one 2p orbital holding a pair, and repulsion between the paired electrons raises the energy of the electron removed. In both cases less energy is needed.

questions.q: The first four successive ionization energies of sodium are 496, 4562, 6910 and 9543 kJ mol⁻¹. Which explanation of the large increase from the first to the second value is correct?
options: The Na⁺ ion has a stable noble-gas octet, and ions resist losing electrons from a complete outer shell.
The second electron is removed from the 2p sublevel, which is closer to the nucleus and less shielded.
After one electron is lost, the fixed pull of the nucleus is shared among 10 electrons, not 11.
Losing the first electron raises the nuclear charge, so the next electron is held far more tightly.
optionWhy: Ions do not 'resist' losing a full shell. The second electron needs far more energy because it is in the second main level, closer to the nucleus and less shielded than the 3s electron.

Sodium is 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s¹. The first electron comes from 3s; the second comes from 2p, in a lower main level, closer to the nucleus and shielded only by the 1s electrons. It is attracted much more strongly, so far more energy is needed.
The nucleus does not share a fixed amount of pull among its electrons. The big increase happens because the second electron is in a lower main level, closer to the nucleus and less shielded.
The nuclear charge depends on the number of protons and stays +11 in Na⁺. The large increase arises because the second electron is removed from 2p, closer to the nucleus and less shielded.
questions.explain: Sodium is 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s¹. The first electron comes from 3s; the second comes from 2p, in a lower main level, closer to the nucleus and shielded only by the 1s electrons. It is attracted much more strongly, so far more energy is needed.
